prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets with endogenous prices, and to analyse dynamic industries, which transformed the empirical measurement of market power and welfare

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. In round 1 I preferred B013 (Autor, Hanson, Katz). I now prefer B001 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn). The reason is not the support counts. It is that the exchange and the chair's questions exposed a problem in my own case that I cannot resolve. I tried to define B013 as a single strand, as the chair asked. A trade-shock-only version (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) has a clean trio, but it drops the skill-demand framework that I argued gives the evidence its wider interpretation, and the magnitudes and persistence of the China shock are the contested part. A skill-and-task-only version rests on Autor and Katz, with substantial credit outside the ballot entry and a closer relation to the 2024 prize than I allowed in round 1. The combined version that I valued needs four names and a three-name cap forces a cut between Katz and Dorn. I can defend each version on merit, but none is both complete and cleanly attributed. B001 does not have this problem. Its maturity is not disputed by anyone in the exchange. The core is a jointly authored result with an identifiable trio, and the citation can be written without apportioning the wider programme. On substance, this is a measurement advance of the kind I weight most heavily as an economic historian. It built a disciplined way to recover substitution patterns, markups and welfare from market data, and it changed what could be asked and answered. It was then used well outside industrial organisation and in regulatory practice, and three decades of critique have tested it. My concrete criterion for separating a method from a discovery is whether it (a) made previously unanswerable counterfactual questions answerable, (b) was adopted outside its home field and in institutional practice, and (c) survived long adversarial use. B001 meets all three on the evidence cited in the exchange. I would keep the citation at method level, on demand estimation and competition with dynamic industries as supporting context, and I would not widen it to every strand.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still toolkit versus discovery. Some members may reasonably weigh a method below a substantive finding about who gains and loses from economic change, which is where my own research interest lies, and B013 speaks to that more directly. Bresnahan's omission is a real cost. His work on measuring market power with differentiated-product demand preceded and framed the later methods, and a method-level citation does not recognise it. Reiss, Benkard and Levin are also left out. A citation that credits only Pakes for dynamic industries leaves part of that strand unrecognised. Applied BLP results are known to be sensitive to numerical implementation, instruments and functional form, so wide adoption does not make every application reliable. I work in economic history, not industrial organisation. I rely on background knowledge for adoption and sensitivity claims and have not independently verified any citation or regulatory-use data.

responses.point: Krusell names Pakes, Berry and Bresnahan for B001. He argues that Bresnahan's new empirical IO and early differentiated-product demand work supplied the lineage the later tools answered, that Levinsohn's role is mostly captured in a single paper, and that a Levinsohn version would not be a scientific error.
responses.response: I take the Bresnahan argument seriously, and in round 1 I listed my own B001 alternative with Levinsohn only because the demand-estimation core is the clearest unit. I still keep Levinsohn. A prize for an identifiable method should credit the authors of the jointly written result that defines it. Excluding a co-author of the central paper is a harder attribution problem than leaving out the pioneer of the agenda around it. I would accept your framing if the Committee chose a programme-level citation, but then I would want the citation reworded for that purpose, and I would regard that as a different prize with a more diffuse credit boundary. Your own acknowledgement that the two versions differ by a close judgement, not by a scientific error, is where I end up too.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B013 first with Autor, Katz and Hanson. She holds that without Katz the prize becomes mostly a trade-shock prize, that the Katz versus Dorn choice is a real attribution decision, and that B001 is the strongest alternative but should not outrank B013 merely on first-place counts.
responses.response: I agree that counts are not merit, and my move does not rest on them. Your point that the explanatory half and the identification half each need their own anchor is the reason I could not find a single-strand B013 I would defend. If the Committee takes B013 later, I would support your Autor, Katz, Hanson reading over a two-name version. I would also say plainly that the combined entry has a four-name credit problem that three names do not solve. That, together with the debate over the China-shock magnitudes, is what moved me, not a doubt about the importance of the work.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B001 first and treats B013 as her leading alternative. She notes that her own B013 trio was Autor, Hanson and Dorn, while mine keeps Katz, which shows the attribution there is less settled than for B001.
responses.response: You are right, and it is a fair reading of my round 1 file. The fact that two sympathetic members land on different third names for B013, while the B001 members converge on one trio, is evidence about how settled the credit is. It is not evidence about the quality of the work. I also agree with your point about robustness: the sensitivities in BLP-type estimation have been probed directly and repeatedly, while for B013 the magnitudes are still being contested. I would keep B013 as the leading alternative and would support it in a later year.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, prefers B001 with Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. He argues for defining the unit narrowly as demand and competition estimation plus dynamic industries, not widening it to production-function or entry work. He accepts that a Committee wanting discovery-type prizes might reasonably reach a different view.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow unit, and I would write the citation that way. It answers the pooling concern from the other B001 members and avoids reopening the attribution problem for every strand. On your reservation about discovery versus toolkit, I think the three-part test I gave above is the right way to put the question to the Committee. On the chair's question about evidence, what would change my mind is systematic evidence that conclusions in merger review or welfare counterfactuals reverse under reasonable alternative implementations, instruments or functional forms. That is a stronger threat than a general statement of sensitivity. I have not seen it in this exchange, and I cannot supply it from my own field.

responses.point: Stromberg prefers B001, keeps B013 as his clear second choice, and asks whether a second achievement could be added within the three-person limit without weakening the citation.
responses.response: I considered it and would not add a second part. With three people in total, a second achievement would force a split of the BLP trio or a thin B013 pair, and either one weakens a citation that is currently tight. A single achievement with three names is the more defensible public configuration. I also agree with you that B013 is the right fallback if B001 stalls, and that is how I list it.

uncertainties: Whether Levinsohn or Bresnahan belongs in the third slot, and whether the Committee prefers a method-level citation or a programme-level one. I would accept either as a reasonable judgement, but they are different prizes.
How much weight a methods-and-tools contribution deserves against a substantive finding about who gains and loses from economic change, and whether my three-part test is the right one.

Whether numerical, instrument and functional-form sensitivities in BLP-type work change real merger-review or welfare conclusions. I cannot assess this beyond background knowledge, and systematic robustness evidence would be needed to change my view.
Whether the China-shock magnitudes and the task framework's relation to the 2024 prize will look more settled in a later year, which would make B013 a stronger candidate.
I have not independently verified citation counts, adoption evidence or regulatory-use claims. They rest on my background knowledge and on colleagues' statements.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile shows no co-authorship, institutional or personal tie to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn or Bresnahan, or to the B013 and B050 names. My research on electrification, railways and labour markets is topically adjacent to B013, and I have moved away from that candidacy, so the adjacency is not driving my configuration. My Lund-based committee colleagues are not candidates on this shortlist. These disclosures are not adjudicated.
